newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage rates fall in week.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage rates fall in week.

text.p: Mortgage rates fell this week as inflation fears eased after the Federal Reserve decided not to raise interest rates last week, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 8.06 percent in the week ended Oct. 4, down from 8.16 percent the previous week. Fifteen-year mortgages also slid to 7.58 percent from 7.68 percent.
One-year adjustable rate mortgage rates dropped to 5.70 percent from 5.82 percent in the week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.57 percent, the 15-year 7.09 percent, and the adjustable loan 5.76 percent.

"The Federal Reserve's decision last week not to raise interest rates reduced inflation fears of many investors, helping interest rates fall this week," said Frank Nothaft, Freddie Mac deputy chief economist.
"Mortgage rates are at affordable levels and we would expect affordability to remain strong for the rest of the year."

On Monday, the Commerce Department reported that U.S. August single-family home sales rose 4.7 percent to an annualized rate of 832,000 units. Also, the Conference Board said Tuesday that U.S. leading indicators rose 0.2 percent in August.
The Labour Department will issue September employment data on Friday.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans, unchanged from last week. Charges on 15-year mortgages fell to 1.6 percent from 1.7 percent, and were unchanged for adjustable loans at 1.4 percent.
Separately, the Mortgage Bankers Association of America said the volume of U.S. mortgage applications fell 3.1 percent in the week ended Sept. 27.
Specifically, the volume of applications to refinance mortgages rose 3.1 percent in the latest survey week, while applications to purchase mortgages declined 4.5 percent.
The seasonally adjusted refinancing index rose 3.1 percent to 271.4 from 263.3 the previous week, the trade group said.
The purchase index fell 4.2 percent to 184.1 in the latest survey from 192.4 in the previous week, it said.
